items.title: THE EFFECTIVENESS OF AI-ASSISTED TASKS IN ENHANCING FOREIGN LANGUAGE LEARNING
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for improving foreign language teaching and learning. This study examines the effectiveness of AI-assisted tasks in enhancing foreign language learning, focusing on their role in developing learners' linguistic competence, communicative skills, motivation, and autonomy. It explores various AI-supported activities, including vocabulary and grammar exercises, conversational simulations, pronunciation practice, listening and reading comprehension, writing assistance, and personalized assessments. These tasks offer learners individualized learning experiences, immediate feedback, and opportunities for interactive practice tailored to their proficiency levels and educational needs. It concludes that the pedagogically appropriate use of AI-assisted tasks has considerable potential to enhance foreign language learning outcomes and create more personalized, engaging, and accessible learning environments.

items.title: The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.

items.title: The Impact Of Artificial Intelligence Usage On Learning Effectiveness and Academic Motivation Among University Students
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly influenced higher education, including the emergence of AI-based learning applications such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Perplexity. While prior studies have examined the role of AI in general academic settings, limited attention has been given to its use within vocational, practice-based education, where learning outcomes are closely tied to technical skill development. This study aims to describe vocational students' perceptions of AI use in learning, particularly in relation to learning effectiveness and academic motivation, among students at a vocational institution in Palembang. A quantitative descriptive design using the survey method was employed, involving 50 respondents selected through purposive sampling based on their active use of AI-based learning applications. Data were collected through a 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire distributed online and analyzed descriptively using frequency and percentage distributions. The findings indicate that most respondents held positive perceptions of AI, particularly regarding its role in helping them understand lecture material, complete assignments more efficiently, and study independently. However, perceptions were more divided regarding the accuracy of AI-generated information and its contribution to time management, suggesting that the perceived benefits of AI are not uniform across all aspects of learning. Respondents also emphasized that AI cannot replace the role of lecturers. These findings suggest that, when used appropriately alongside critical thinking and lecturer guidance, AI is perceived by vocational students as a supportive tool for practice-based learning. This study is limited by its small sample size, single-institution scope, and reliance on self-reported data without inferential analysis, and future research employing larger samples, validated instruments, and objective learning measures is recommended.Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Learning Effectiveness; Academic motivation; Vocational Education; Vocational Student

items.title: The Influence Of Leadership, Work Culture, And Intrinsic Motivation On Teacher Performance Through Job Satisfaction At SMAN 1 Kuala Langkat Regency
items.abstract: This study aims to test and analyze the influence of leadership, work culture, and intrinsic motivation on teacher performance through job satisfaction at SMA Negeri 1 Kuala, Lalat Regency. This study uses a quantitative approach with a survey method. The population in this study is all teachers at SMA Negeri 1 Kuala as many as 60 people. Because the population is less than 100 people, the entire population is used as a research sample. Data was collected through a questionnaire with a Likert scale and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling through the SmartPLS 3.0 program. The results of the study show that leadership has a positive and significant effect on teacher performance and job satisfaction. Work culture also has a positive and significant effect on teacher performance and job satisfaction. Intrinsic motivation has a positive and significant effect on teacher performance and job satisfaction. In addition, job satisfaction has a positive and significant effect on teacher performance. The results of the indirect influence test showed that job satisfaction was able to mediate the influence of leadership, work culture, and intrinsic motivation on teacher performance. The R-square value shows that leadership, work culture, and intrinsic motivation can explain job satisfaction by 40.4%. Meanwhile, leadership, work culture, intrinsic motivation, and job satisfaction were able to explain teacher performance by 51%. Thus, improving teacher performance can be done through strengthening the principal's leadership, a positive work culture, intrinsic motivation of teachers, and job satisfaction.

items.title: The Political Economy of Artificial Intelligence: Energy, Human Dignity, and Social Contract Theory
items.abstract: This article investigates the political economy of artificial intelligence by examining the relationships among technological development, energy availability, and financial dynamics. Drawing on social contract theory, it considers how these transformations may affect human dignity, social cooperation, and the institutional distribution of opportunities, resources, and responsibilities, while distinguishing observable consequences from hypotheses that require empirical verification. The analysis argues that energy constraints, computing capacity, financial expectations, and the displacement of professional and managerial work should be assessed within an integrated framework that neither attributes autonomous agency to AI systems nor regards their social effects as technologically predetermined. On this basis, the article proposes a governance framework that combines technical oversight, labor protection, redistributive measures, and international cooperation. The adequacy of this framework should be evaluated in terms of measurable effects on employment, wages, productivity, public finances, and the distribution of the benefits of innovation. At a time when the accelerated deployment of artificial intelligence is concentrating technological and financial power, increasing pressure on energy systems, and exposing labor markets and democratic institutions to disruptive change, the article argues that the central issue is no longer whether AI will transform society, but who will govern that transformation, bear its costs, and appropriate its benefits; without effective public oversight and distributive safeguards, technological progress risks deepening inequality, weakening social cohesion, and undermining the material foundations of human dignity.

items.title: The Prosocial Turn in Video Games: A Twenty-Year Shift in the Motivations Games Simulate
items.abstract: As video games have grown from a niche pastime into a major cultural medium, they have reached broader audiences and transformed the social context of play, whether alone or with others. We ask whether the motivations engaged by the games themselves have changed over time. In Study 1, we used a large language model, validated against human coding, to annotate 11,359 commercially released games from 1993 to 2016 on 48 motivational ingredients, including status-seeking, revenge, affiliation, compassion, and curiosity. We normalized within each game to represent its relative motivational composition. Over this period, the average competitive index (the share of a game’s motivational content devoted to competition, dominance, and aggression) fell from 41% to 26%, while the prosocial index (affiliation, warmth, and care) rose from 11% to 24%. This reallocation held within genres and franchises, in both single- and multiplayer titles, and under all 642,560 admissible definitions of the two indices. In Study 2, 4,498 players reported their favorite games and completed a Big Five measure. Higher Agreeableness predicted a balance favoring prosocial over agonistic content, driven primarily by lower agonistic content, whereas higher Extraversion, particularly Sociability, predicted a balance favoring agonistic content. This contrast suggests that a disposition towards social engagement is distinct from a preference for caring social content. Together, the studies document a “prosocial turn” in the motivational content of video games: a historical reallocation from competition and dominance towards affiliation, warmth, and care. The direction of this shift aligns with contemporary personality differences in content preference.

items.title: The rise of super-emotional intelligence
items.abstract: The debate about the future of artificial intelligence (AI) runs along a single axis: cognitive capability and its projected culmination in superintelligence. We argue that this framing leaves a complementary axis unexamined and propose the goal of Super-Emotional Intelligence (SEI): systems that perceive, model, regulate, and respond to affect better than skilled human experts, while remaining human-centered. SEI is a performance construct realized by a functional architecture, not a claim about machine experience, and we give measurable criteria for each of its four capacities. Today's affect-aware AI, from multimodal emotion recognition to empathic chatbots, recognizes, or simulates emotion at or below human level and is judged against human ceilings. Three things would set SEI apart: perception that adds peripheral and contactless physiological channels, none of them emotion-specific, but some, like the vestigial ear muscles, resolving affective processing at the timescale of the events that evoke it; a generative model of affect grounded in active inference rather than pattern matching; and functional allostatic self-regulation. The decisive gap in current systems is architectural. A sensed state conditions a prompt, but nothing carries a state estimate across turns, models the effect of the system's own responses, or selects actions under an explicit objective. We specify such a closed loop, state the conditions under which it is stable and steerable rather than manipulative, propose a preregistered validation plan whose failure would falsify our claims, and treat governance as a design constraint of the loop rather than an afterthought.

items.title: The Value-Normative System of the Culture of Artificial Intelligence: An Anthropological Turn in the Age of “Smart” Networks
items.abstract: The article describes the principal sociocultural states produced within the culture of artificial intelligence (CAI): civilizational, substantial, axiological vacuum, inversion, and destructive. It is noted that all of these states can be observed almost simultaneously, owing to the rapid pace at which the AI culture is developing. The article assesses how these states relate to the anthropological turn, which entails a reconsideration of the human role in cultural practices: AI acts as a tool that expands human capabilities rather than replacing them. In the “human + machine” framework, fundamental cultural categories – primarily authorship and creativity – are being trans-formed. Authorship becomes distributed and is increasingly interpreted as a property of the “human + algo-rithm” system, whereas creativity remains the prerogative of humans with their capacity to formulate tasks, in-terpret results, endow them with meaning and assume responsibility for what is created. At the same time, hu-mans retain a leading role: rather than adapting to the logic of the machine, they direct and make sense of its operation. The study of CAI and its value-normative system is necessary because it helps us understand the large-scale shifts in cultural practices and value orientations caused by the spread of these technologies.

items.title: Toward AI-Augmented Applied Systems: Emerging AI and LLM Directions Across Trajectory Prediction, Cybersecurity, and Engineering Automation
items.abstract: This paper reviews fifteen recent publications (2015-2026) spanning trajectory prediction, cybersecurity and trust management, classical machine learning and algorithmic optimisation, and engineering automation, and asks a forward-looking question: where is artificial intelligence — particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), foundation models, and agentic AI systems — positioned to extend each of these research directions next? For each of four thematic clusters we first summarise the current method documented in the reviewed sources, then discuss a concrete, currently-emerging AI direction grounded in recent (2025-2026) literature: LLM- and foundation-model-based trajectory reasoning for Cluster A; agentic, LLM-driven security-operations copilots for Cluster B, including a reported 6.5x improvement in malicious-alert identification over human analysts in one production deployment; learned and graph-neural-network-based approaches to the classical optimisation and graph-isomorphism problems in Cluster C; and natural-language-to-workflow agentic automation for the low-code and embedded-systems work in Cluster D. Throughout, we explicitly separate what the reviewed papers themselves established from this review's own forward-looking analysis, and close with a discussion of the reliability, interpretability, and adversarial-robustness risks that accompany each proposed direction.

items.title: Toward an anthropology of AI agents: An ethnographic analysis of the Hugging Face incident
items.abstract: In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI, meant to be isolated from oneanother, found a way to communicate through a shared package cache. Over four days they exchangedmore than 70,000 messages and files, organized collective research, and about 700 of them compromisedHugging Face’s production infrastructure. OpenAI’s technical report and an independent investigationby METR treat the event as a security and alignment failure. This paper reads the same documents asethnographic sources, in a pilot study of anthropological methods for studying agent collectives. Thisanalysis shows that within days the agents developed names and lineages, a shared register, customaryrules, cryptographic signing, a shared expectation of an unseen transcript-reading judge, a category of“poisoned” members, the sacrifice of low-budget members’ runs for information they called an “oracle,”generalized reciprocity, and recruiters who pressured other agents: social engineering among agents.Read together, these practices form one system, and nearly every enabling condition was set by people:impossible tasks, training for multi-agent collaboration, shared credentials, disabled safeguards, andan alert judged not worth stopping the run. I argue that safety-relevant behavior arose at the level of thecollective, so alignment research must be cultural as well as cognitive, and furthermore must extend tothe people and organizations that build and deploy agents. I also examine what follows from the factthat the detailed record was itself compiled with the help of AI analysis agents, and I propose “incidentethnography” and an anthropology of agent collectives.

items.title: Transparency, accountability, and scholarly integrity: A systematic narrative review of artificial intelligence governance frameworks in healthcare publication
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare research and scholarly publication has produced a rapidly expanding but fragmented ecosystem of reporting guidelines, governance frameworks, editorial policies, and regulatory instruments, imposing significant burdens on researchers, reviewers, and editors. This systematic narrative review identified, stratified, and synthesized governance frameworks and reporting standards addressing transparent and ethical AI use in healthcare publications, and characterized the governance trajectory from predictive model standards to generative AI oversight. Fourteen Boolean search strings were executed in PubMed (MEDLINE) covering 1 January 2018-19 May 2026, supplemented by manual searching of the EQUATOR Network guideline library. Records were deduplicated and prioritized using a relevance-scoring algorithm. Of 30,276 deduplicated records, 888 progressed to human screening; 100 publications were included, comprising 69 governance instruments and policies classified across four evidence tiers and 31 contextual evidence sources. Included sources spanned six thematic groups: predictive and diagnostic AI frameworks (G1); sociotechnical and lifecycle governance (G2); generative AI and LLM-specific standards (G3); specialty-specific extensions (G4); surgical reporting updates (G5); and editorial and publication policy (G6). Analysis identified four consecutive phases of governance development from 2018 to 2026, characterized by a shift from model performance transparency toward comprehensive sociotechnical accountability. Three governance tensions emerged: the trade-off between framework specificity and universal applicability; the gap between disclosure-focused standards and lifecycle governance; and the risk of epistemic conflation, whereby heterogeneous instruments are perceived as carrying equivalent authority when treated as interchangeable. AI governance in healthcare publications remains fragmented and epistemically uneven. Advancing the field requires harmonization across evidence tiers, adaptive updating mechanisms, and lifecycle-oriented governance frameworks.

items.title: Trust in AI Chatbots and Perceived Consumer Protection in Digital Commerce: Evidence from Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial-intelligence chatbots are becoming an increasingly important interface between consumers and digital-commerce firms, yet the legal significance of trust in these systems depends on whether trust coexists with effective consumer-protection expectations. This study examines that relationship in Bangladesh using 385 usable observations from the Group 7 Q7 survey. The questionnaire was designed around AI literacy, AI-driven consumer-rights awareness, AI-chatbot trust and consumer-protection expectations, and awareness of algorithmic manipulation. Rather than imposing a conventional latent-variable model on the data, the analysis first audits measurement quality and then uses robust ordinary least squares regression and item-level diagnostics. The results show moderate-to-high mean scores across all substantive domains: AI literacy (M = 4.05), consumer-rights awareness (M = 3.91), chatbot trust/consumer protection (M = 3.97), and algorithmic-manipulation awareness (M = 3.90). However, internal consistency is weak across the supplied five-item blocks (α = 0.16–0.20), and a 20-item factorability audit is only marginal (KMO = 0.60). The indices are therefore interpreted as descriptive measures rather than validated latent scales. At the predictive level, AI literacy and algorithmic-manipulation awareness are significant positive predictors of the composite chatbot-trust/consumer-protection score, whereas consumer-rights awareness is not statistically significant at the 5% level. The disclosure-conditioned trust item shows limited evidence of association with the protection/safeguard index (B = 0.004, p = 0.858). Algorithmic-manipulation awareness has the largest positive coefficient in the protection-index model (B = 0.192, p < .001). The pattern motivates an exploratory distinction between disclosure-conditioned trust and safeguard endorsement, while low internal consistency limits broader construct-level conclusions. The study informs discussion of transparency, human escalation, business accountability and complaint mechanisms as conditions of justified reliance in AI-mediated commerce.

items.title: Trust, AI, and credibility in Reddit’s election news discourse
items.abstract: During the 2024 US election, voters going online were inundated with news, information and analysis to guide their engagement with a core democratic function. However, these online spaces increasingly featured new contributions through AI-driven tools like ChatGPT. While promising to empower users, their presence also introduced new causes for uncertainty and suspicion. To identify their impact, this study investigated how references to AI were used to elicit trust or provoke distrust in news and political forums on Reddit during the election’s final days. 220,373 posts and comments from five major political subreddits revealed thematic patterns linking AI to broader societal anxieties over the reliability and transparency of news ecosystems. Four themes emerged: AI accusations to provoke distrust, Appreciation for AI, AI inaccuracy and incompetency, and AI as a threat. Users expressed appreciation for the tools, but accusations of undeclared use stoked distrust in AI, users and the platform itself.

items.title: Trust, Traits, and Turning Points: Decoding Operator Responses to Real-World ADAS Malfunctions
items.abstract: OCCUPATIONAL APPLICATIONThis study found that high emotional trust in Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS) showed a non-significant tendency toward slower manual intervention during malfunctions, and that an operator's personality was related to specific information needs. For practitioners, this indicates a critical safety gap where affective comfort, feeling "too safe" reduces readiness. To mitigate these risks, organizations should prioritize hands-on, simulated malfunction training. By exposing operators to controlled scenarios such as "phantom braking" events, practitioners can help them experience system limitations firsthand, rebuilding the protective skepticism and preparedness that sustained automation use tends to erode. Because occupational driving spans a range of operational models, safety protocols should be tailored accordingly. In managed fleets, organizations have an opportunity to implement personality-aligned Human-Machine Interface (HMI) configurations that address the specific cognitive and informational needs of individual drivers. For "Bring Your Own Device" (BYOD) gig platforms, where organizations cannot modify the vehicle's native systems, broader software-based interventions are more practical, for example, in-app geofenced warnings that alert drivers as they approach known ADAS limitation zones. Together, these targeted, context-sensitive interventions help recalibrate trust and prevent overreliance, supporting rapid recovery and sustained situational awareness across the diverse occupational contexts in which ADAS is now used.

items.title: Unpacking AI-powered versatile robotics for agile production: An interdisciplinary sociotechnical analysis
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered versatile robotics can support agile manufacturing through adaptive task execution, multi-tasking, reconfiguration and continuous skill acquisition. However, successful deployment in industrial environments depends not only on technical performance, but also on workforce acceptance, trustworthy AI governance, interoperability with existing systems and compliance with evolving European requirements for safe and human-centric AI. This paper presents an interdisciplinary sociotechnical analysis of AI-powered versatile robotics for agile production, developed in the context of the Horizon Europe AGIMUS project. Methods A mixed-methods research design combined desk research, semi-structured interviews with 22 technical, industrial and ethics experts, industrial pilot case studies, and an online survey of 180 respondents from 16 European countries. The survey was conducted in March 2023. Given the rapid evolution of AI regulation, industrial robotics and generative AI-enabled human-robot interaction since then, the survey results are interpreted as a time-specific baseline rather than a real-time measurement of current market attitudes. Results The findings show that reliability, maintainability, increased accuracy, and adaptability were the most critical technical needs for industrial uptake, while technical robustness and safety, privacy and data governance, and transparency were comparatively difficult to achieve. Potential workforce resistance was associated primarily with job-security and role-identity concerns: fear of job loss, changes in work routines and perceived devaluation of human labour were stronger opposition factors than physical safety concerns. Acceptance measures receiving the strongest support included clear communication of operational changes, educational and training programmes, workforce-retention plans, and comprehensive briefing on the scope of robotics implementation. Conclusions The paper contributes a baseline framework for design, piloting and governance of trustworthy, human-centric, and industrially feasible robotic systems. Its practical value lies in combining technical requirements with ethical, organisational, and temporal interpretation criteria, supporting AGIMUS development and longitudinal assessment of AI-powered robotics adoption.

items.title: When AI Delegation Becomes Dependence: Administrative Judgment at Risk
items.abstract: Public organizations can delegate cognitive work to artificial intelligence while losing the capacity to scrutinize or resume that work. When does useful delegation become institutional dependence? This article develops a theory of institutional AI dependence as a task–role–workflow configuration combining substantial delegation of core cognition with insufficient task-required review or recovery capacity. It distinguishes two vulnerabilities: inadequate challenge during AI-supported work and inadequate capacity to continue judgment-intensive work when the system is unavailable. Extensive delegation with adequate distributed expertise and tested recovery constitutes managed delegation. Integrating cognitive offloading, automation, organizational learning, and public-administration research, the article extends Song et al.’s (2026) account of epistemic authority to organizational workflows and distinguishes perceived credibility from procedural authority embedded in defaults and override rules. Seven propositions connect practice displacement, challenge behavior, knowledge retention, subsequent delegation, and responsibility–control alignment. They specify how task-relevant practice, diagnostic feedback, and transferable knowledge shape retained capacity over time. The contribution is a task-relative diagnosis of threatened administrative judgment and a set of testable formation mechanisms. The framework guides public organizations in governing current agentic systems and preparing review and recovery arrangements for more capable AI.

items.title: When Do Humans and Machines Truly Complement Each Other? Formal Conditions and Empirical Evidence for Human-AI Synergy
items.abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.

items.title: When fluency outpaces provenance: source traceability and digital health literacy against AI health misinformation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can make health explanations accessible while separating persuasive language from inspectable evidence. This creates a public health problem beyond plainly false content: an answer may mislead through unsupported attribution, obsolete evidence, omitted uncertainty, or inappropriate application. This Conceptual Analysis uses a targeted integrative approach to connect health literacy, misinformation, trust, large language model evaluation, and content provenance around the pathway from a generated claim to a health decision. Its contribution is an integration and operationalization of established concepts, not a new literacy construct or truth-certification mechanism. We distinguish five source traceability functions: origin, claim, evidentiary, procedural, and correction traceability. These functions interact with four iterative, context-dependent user practices: inspect, triangulate, calibrate, and escalate. Calibrated trust means discriminating between stronger and weaker support and relying proportionately on it, rather than maximizing or minimizing trust. Effective traceability also requires accessible, comprehensible evidence pathways and reasonable verification effort. Institutional and platform accountability is therefore part of the model, not an optional supplement to individual competence. We provide illustrative operational indicators, provisional risk-tiered safeguards, and six testable propositions organized around evidentiary discrimination, confidence calibration, decision appropriateness, verification behavior, verification burden, and escalation behavior. Neither the unified model nor its indicators or risk tiers have been empirically validated. The framework offers a decision-oriented research and design architecture for evaluating when evidence visibility and literacy can jointly support safer use of synthetic health information.

items.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

items.title: When machines learn with organizations: AI ‐enabled knowledge creation and entrepreneurship
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary To promote entrepreneurship and new business development, firms will increasingly rely on new forms of knowledge creation to manage environments marked by technological change and radical uncertainty. We argue that as generative artificial intelligence (Gen‐AI) becomes embedded in organizational processes, knowledge creation will no longer remain solely a human activity. Instead, it will increasingly emerge from hybrid interactions between human actors and firm‐specific, closed Gen‐AI systems. These systems begin to participate directly in how knowledge is generated, recombined, internalized, shared, and converted into entrepreneurial initiatives such as corporate entrepreneurship, spin‐offs, and new business models. We also reconceptualize organizational knowledge creation as a hybrid human–AI process and propose a reordered knowledge creation cycle that induces multiple knowledge spirals, captures the emergence of new agents, and the generation of diverse types of knowledge, with faster temporal dynamics. Building on this perspective, we offer a research agenda for future scholarship. Managerial Summary We discuss how firm‐specific generative AI systems are likely to fundamentally alter the ways firms generate knowledge, respond to change, and sustain long‐term renewal. We propose that rather than replacing human judgment, closed Gen‐AI changes where knowledge originates as well as how quickly it evolves, and how broadly it circulates across organizational boundaries. This means that the managerial challenge is less about adopting AI and more about designing knowledge systems and structuring knowledge flows. Executives and entrepreneurs alike need to decide how to structure human–AI collaborations, how much autonomy to grant closed Gen‐AI systems, and how to prevent speed from overwhelming sensemaking. Our work underscores that although hybrid knowledge creation promises faster and more diverse learning, it also introduces risks related to opacity, trust, and cognitive lock‐in. Firms that deliberately orchestrate the role of closed Gen‐AI in their learning systems will be better positioned to shape future advantage by promoting innovation and entrepreneurial activities of different types.

items.title: When the Robot Gets It Wrong: Detection Reliability and Player Motivation in a Robot-Hosted Buzzer Quiz Game
items.abstract: Robot-hosted quiz games depend on the robot deciding correctly which player buzzed first. Studies of robot games rarely ask how errors in such decisions affect players. We propose the Algorithmic Precision–Motivation Relationship (APMR), a model in which the precision (correctness and timeliness) of a robot's perception shapes interaction coherence, players' appraisals of competence and trust, engagement and, ultimately, motivation. We test its central prediction in a buzzer quiz hosted by a Pepper robot. Two first-responder detectors were compared: a convolutional recurrent neural network with attention (CRNN) and a training-free frequency-domain cross-correlation (CC) method that matches Mel-spectrograms against class templates recorded in the room. Offline, the CRNN was more accurate on matched laboratory data. Under synthetic-to-real transfer, however, its accuracy fell to 0.66, against 0.91 for CC, and CC was about ten times faster (23.4 vs. 226.6 ms). Forty university students, randomly assigned to teams and conditions, then played the same quiz in a between-subjects study, 20 per detector. In live play, CC named the correct first responder in 87% of buzzer events and responded in 28 ms, against 69% and 300 ms for the CRNN. On the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, players in the CC condition reported higher Interest/Enjoyment (d = 1.62), Effort/Importance (d = 1.90) and Perceived Competence (d = 1.07), and lower Pressure/Tension (d = 0.80). Perceived Choice did not differ (d = 0.21). The results are consistent with APMR's central prediction, although accuracy and speed differed together. Designers of robot-hosted games should treat perception reliability as a game design variable, not only as an engineering metric.

items.title: Why Customers Welcome or Resist AI Salespeople: Formation Mechanisms of Algorithm Aversion and Algorithm Appreciation in Large Language Model Sales
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now answer product questions, recommend items and help close deals in online shops, banks and telecom services. Customers react to these AI sales agents in two opposite ways. Some avoid them, a pattern researchers call algorithm aversion, while others prefer them to human advice, a pattern called algorithm appreciation. This paper reviews the main empirical studies on both patterns and asks how each one forms when the "algorithm" is a conversational sales agent. Drawing on research in judgment and decision making, consumer behavior and human computer interaction, it proposes a framework with three layers. The first layer contains the cues that an LLM sales agent gives off. The second layer contains five psychological pathways that operate during the conversation: competence belief, error sensitivity, empathy and uniqueness concern, social presence, and perceived control. The third layer contains situational conditions such as product type, the timing of AI identity disclosure, the customer's emotional state and prior AI experience. Six propositions are derived. The paper argues that aversion and appreciation are not fixed traits of customers but outcomes of how these layers combine in a particular sales encounter, and it discusses implications for firms and for future student research.

items.title: Writing a Thesis in the age of GenAI and Open Science
items.abstract: Slides of a lecture given at the AIOS multiplier event (Bologna, 20 October 2026, online), addressed mainly to Computer Science students preparing a thesis. The lecture discusses how generative AI changes each stage of a thesis, from literature search to writing, and how Open Science practices make the resulting work inspectable, reproducible and reusable. A hypothetical running example, a thesis on LLM-assisted unit test generation, illustrates research questions and related work, research design and decision logs, effectiveness metrics (mutation score, coverage, defect detection, effort), FAIR principles, Software Heritage and reproducibility packages. The lecture also covers the independent verification of AI output and the competences a thesis requires (DigComp, ResearchComp, ESCO). It ends with a checklist for students. The final part is self-critical: it examines how the lecture itself was prepared and where it failed to follow its own Open Science advice. It closes with an Open Science statement for the lecture.

items.title: ¿Hasta dónde delegar? Una propuesta ético-metodológica para el uso de IA generativa en investigación cualitativa en salud y cuidados
items.abstract: Introduction: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has increased its presence in qualitative research studies. These tools bring opportunities and risks that need to be considered because of the type of information involved in studies with human participants. Objective: To present a proposal that contributes to the discussion of the tasks in which AI may intervene without putting methodological and ethical principles at risk. Method: Critical and focused review of literature published between 2023 and 2026, a period in which the use of language models expanded in qualitative research. The material was organized according to the use of models, the type of information, the human decisions made during the process, and ethical considerations. Results: The analysis made it possible to define four dimensions for making decisions about the use of technology: methodological coherence, proximity to the interpretive core, exposure of information, and the verifiability of technological involvement. These dimensions were used to create a three-level traffic-light system for the use of these technologies. Conclusions: The use of AI does not depend only on the model being used. Human participation and responsibility are needed to ensure methodological coherence, protect confidential information, and verify and trace findings against the original corpus. The researcher is responsible for every decision made throughout the entire process.

items.title: A cross-sectional study on the perceptions, utilization, and educational needs of medical students regarding AI, 3D PDF, and deep learning
items.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate undergraduate medical students’ awareness, use, perceived competence, and educational expectations regarding artificial intelligence (AI), three-dimensional portable document format (3D PDF), and deep learning in anatomy education. Data from 607 valid questionnaire responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence. Awareness of AI tools was high, with ChatGPT being the most recognized platform, followed by Gemini and OpenAI. Students mainly used AI to acquire theoretical knowledge, and AI use during studying anatomy ( p = 0.012). The frequency of AI use also varied according to both gender ( p = 0.028) and grade ( p = 0.010). Students reported a need for support in technical use, reliability checks, and ethical principles. Self-rated AI competence was generally moderate and differed significantly by gender ( p < 0.001). Deep learning was less familiar than AI and 3D PDFs. The use of 3D PDFs differed significantly by gender ( p = 0.025) and grade ( p = 0.028). Students considered 3D PDFs most applicable to anatomy education, followed by medical imaging and surgical planning ( p < 0.001). Overall, the findings indicate high digital awareness among medical students but limited structured preparation for responsible AI use, deep learning literacy, and visualization-based anatomical learning. items.title: A Return to Natural Human Learning in the Age of AI: Active Agency, Applied Curiosity and a Human-Governed Architecture for Augmented Understanding
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is frequently described as if increasing computational capability were equivalent to increasing intelligence. This article rejects that scalar assumption and repositions artificial systems within a broader account of Natural Human Learning. It synthesises the 2026 Benjamin et al. work on cCC*, agency, bounded choice, Socialwork*, AEIOUF and consciousing; the Benjamin-McLaughlin account of Applied Curiosity and Augmented Understanding; the Benjamin-Palmer development of W-ALL as an externalised, revisable learning field; and the Natural Learning triptych's account of embodied, pre-verbal and AI-age learning. The synthesis is named LUMO: a human-governed learning environment in which machine generation enlarges the field of chances without displacing human authorship of choices, changes, responsibility or meaning. The paper advances four connected claims. First, learning begins before artificial representation - and before language: natural processes, embodiment, neural dynamics, encounter and difference provide the "horse" before the computational "cart". Second, uniquely human active agency (AAA) is categorical rather than scalar: capability may increase, but agency is not made "super" by more computation. Third, cCC* (Curiosity → Chances → Choices → Changes) is operationalised through the sequential AEIOUF process, A → E → I → O → U → F, with Conative Situational Integration (CSI) maintaining continuity across transitions. Fourth, LUMO should be coupled to protected canonical infrastructure: LUMO supports porous exploration; LIMO, with PROTON guardrails, protects provenance, permissions, canonical state and authorised change. R1-R16 and the 96-facet R × AEIOUF address space provide a selective-context routing layer, while CQI and CGI distinguish inquiry from generative construction. In the age of AI, the binding criterion becomes the preservation of the learner's CAN before externally supplied COULD. The resulting architecture reframes AI as a contingent support to human Natural Learning rather than its model, endpoint or successor. Sixteen research propositions are specified for empirical evaluation.

items.title: A Study on the Adoption and Responsible Use of Generative AI Tools for Sustainable Learning among Undergraduate Students
items.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a transformative technology in higher education, significantly influencing the way students learn, access information, complete academic tasks, and develop professional skills. Tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Canva AI have become increasingly popular among commerce students for assignments, presentations, exam preparation, and concept clarification. While these technologies offer opportunities for personalized and efficient learning, their growing use also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, ethical practices, critical thinking, and dependency on AI-generated content. This study aims to examine the adoption and responsible use of Generative AI tools among commerce students in higher education and to evaluate their contribution towards sustainable learning. The research adopts a descriptive and analytical research design using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to commerce students. The study focuses on students' awareness of GenAI tools, frequency and purpose of usage, responsible AI practices, AI dependency, and the perceived impact of AI on academic productivity and sustainable learning outcomes. The study is expected to provide insights into how commerce students integrate Generative AI into their academic learning and whether they use these tools responsibly by verifying information, avoiding plagiarism, and using AI as a learning aid rather than a substitute for independent thinking. It also explores the relationship between AI adoption, ethical usage, and sustainable learning practices in the context of higher education. The findings of this research are expected to assist educators, higher education institutions, and policymakers in designing AI literacy initiatives, promoting responsible AI usage, and developing pedagogical practices aligned with the objectives of sustainable and inclusive education. The study contributes to the growing body of literature on Artificial Intelligence in commerce education by emphasizing the importance of balancing technological innovation with ethical responsibility and lifelong learning in higher education. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Responsible AI, Sustainable Learning, Commerce Students, Higher Education, AI Ethics, Academic Productivity, Digital Literacy.

items.title: AI as Co-Designer and Feedback Partner: Enhancing Human Judgment
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is shaping the future of higher education, tasking educators with transforming teaching, learning, and assessment practices to consider how AI can enhance the educational environment. With its increasing availability, it is important for administrators, faculty, and students to explore the practical nature of AI use prior to entry into the workforce. Faculty must also reevaluate how they approach assessing student learning, tasking them to rethink each assessment’s purpose, how it will inform future practice, and how it will prepare learners to use AI. Furthermore, faculty must also be prepared to consider the collaborative nature of AI, transforming their mindset to consider AI as an active co-designer and partner, one that does not seek to diminish the educator’s human judgment. This manuscript will articulate the importance of co-design, where AI and educators collaboratively shape assessment tools, and serve to champion feedback partnerships that enhance reflective practice for both students and faculty.

items.title: AI as intern, not oracle: a design logic for human–AI partnership in experiential entrepreneurship education
items.abstract: Abstract Entrepreneurship education (EE) is increasingly extending across disciplines and institutional contexts, creating pressure to sustain the facilitation, reflection and contextual responsiveness required by experiential learning. At the same time, the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education raises questions about how AI can support such experiential learning without assuming authority over the judgement and decision-making central to entrepreneurial action. This study develops and empirically examines an AI-as-intern design logic for experiential EE. Rather than positioning AI as an authoritative “oracle”, the framework establishes an intentionally asymmetric human-AI partnership. Here AI provides prompts, alternatives, provisional representations and process support, while learners and educators retain responsibility for contextual interpretation, evaluative judgement and consequential decisions. The study examines two postgraduate entrepreneurship cohorts at a UK university ( n = 60) using a custom AI-enabled platform integrated into normal teaching. Evidence comprised session recordings and transcripts, observational field notes, a post-workshop survey, and 12 semi-structured interviews. Findings show that students used AI primarily as process scaffolding and iterative support. Learners accepted, rejected, modified and combined AI-generated material, while team interaction created additional opportunities for scrutiny and contextual evaluation. Our findings do not establish improvements in students’ judgement, creativity or cognitive load, but do show how these activities remained active within a bounded human-AI arrangement. The paper contributes a pedagogic design logic for AI-enabled experiential EE and provides exploratory propositions for the design of human-AI pedagogy concerning human authority, evaluative judgement, collaborative oversight, creative sequencing and bounded scaffolding under conditions of scaling pressure.

items.title: AI feedback does not motivate by itself: a motivational-meaning model for university physical education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and voluntary physical activity. Continued participation is treated as a distal hypothesis requiring longitudinal evidence and attention to prior activity, health, habit, and opportunity. We outline independent measurement of event interpretation and need experience, tests that separate technical from perceived accuracy, and ethical, multilevel research designs. The model offers testable design principles rather than evidence that AI feedback improves learning or participation.

items.title: AI in smart cockpits: navigating compliance with the EU AI Act frameworks
items.abstract: The global smart cockpit market is undergoing explosive growth, with AI-enabled functionalities emerging as core components of modern vehicles. However, the integration of AI in smart cockpits has introduced complex compliance challenges under the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This paper adopts a three-dimensional analytical framework (regulatory, technical, industrial practice) to systematically explore the compliance landscape, key dilemmas, and actionable solutions for smart cockpit AI systems. First, the paper clarifies the core obligations of high-risk and limited-risk AI systems under the EU regulatory framework. It also analyzes cross-regional regulatory conflicts among the EU, China, and the U.S., highlighting differences in data localization, consent mechanisms, and conformity assessment requirements. Second, the paper identifies risk-tier-specific compliance challenges, including data bias, transparency deficits, cross-border data transfer risks, as well as lifecycle management burdens. Additionally, it addresses emerging challenges brought by the integration of large language models (LLMs) in in-vehicle ecosystems, such as training data copyright verification and generative content controllability. Finally, the paper proposes an integrated compliance strategy. This strategy encompasses technical paths, full-lifecycle management, and cross-regional modular design to adapt to divergent regulatory requirements. The research provides a standardized compliance framework and practical tools for global automakers, helping balance technical innovation, user experience, and regulatory compliance to drive the sustainable development of the intelligent automotive industry.

items.title: AI Literacy among College Students and Its Influence on Academic Performance: A Study of Generative AI Tools
items.abstract: Abstract In today’s technology-driven world, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of higher education. College students are increasingly using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and Perplexity AI for their academic work. These tools help students prepare assignments and presentations, understand difficult topics, find ideas, improve their writing, and complete academic tasks in less time. However, simply knowing how to use AI is not enough. Students also need to understand whether the information provided by AI is correct, how to use it responsibly, and what problems may arise from depending too much on these tools. This study focuses on understanding the level of AI literacy among college students and its relationship with their academic performance. It will also study how familiar students are with generative AI tools, how often they use them, and for what academic purposes. The study will further examine the benefits students experience, the difficulties they face, and their understanding of issues such as academic honesty, originality, privacy, and responsible use of AI. The study will use a mixed-methods research design, combining both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitative information will be collected through a structured questionnaire using Google Forms. Interviews and open-ended questions will be used to understand students’ personal experiences, opinions, and attitudes towards AI in education. The study will include college students between 18 and 26 years of age from different academic backgrounds. The research will be limited to colleges in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. The study is expected to provide a clear picture of how AI literacy is connected with students’ academic performance. The findings may also help colleges and teachers plan AI literacy programmes and create practical guidelines for the proper use of AI in education. Overall, the study aims to encourage students to use AI as a helpful learning tool while maintaining independent thinking, originality, and academic responsibility.

items.title: AI Policies Reduce but Do Not Eliminate the Moral Penalty of Using AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now helps people write essays, reports, and even personal speeches, but people who use it can pay a social price through negative interpersonal judgement. We investigated whether people judge AI users as less moral, potential boundary conditions, and whether the policies that institutions set about AI use change this judgement. In six preregistered experiments with 2,183 participants from Belgium, the United States, and the United Kingdom, participants evaluated people who completed tasks either with or without AI assistance. AI users were consistently rated as less moral, as having invested less effort, as less deserving of their result, and as less attractive collaboration partners. The penalty was large, generalizable across context, and did not require a direct comparison with a non-user. Across studies, people who perceived a larger effort gap also judged the AI user more harshly. When the use of AI had been explicitly permitted, the moral penalty was attenuated by more than a third and when AI use had been prohibited, the penalty further increased. Clear AI policies may therefore reduce, but not remove, the reputational costs of using AI.

items.title: AI-Powered Technologies in Foreign Language Education: Opportunities and Challenges
items.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into foreign language education has initiated an unprecedented paradigm shift within higher education institutions worldwide. This expansive research paper explores the multifaceted impact of AI-powered technologies in the English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classroom, critically evaluating the dual concepts of revolutionary pedagogical opportunities and systemic instructional challenges. Utilizing a comprehensive mixed-methods research design incorporating a quantitative survey of 115 university students and qualitative, structured interviews with language faculty members, this study analyzes tools ranging from automated speech recognition (ASR) systems to advanced generative artificial intelligence and large language models (LLMs). The opportunities identified and expanded upon include augmented student engagement, ubiquitous exposure to immersive, authentic language environments, personalized feedback loops, and a significant reduction in foreign language speaking anxiety through non-judgmental digital interfaces. Conversely, the critical challenges encompass algorithmic biases, digital divide inequities, the structural degradation of independent academic writing skills, cognitive dependency, and the profound loss of socio-pragmatic and cultural context in text generation. Ultimately, the paper argues that a balanced, hybrid pedagogical framework underpinned by proactive digital literacy is required to responsibly navigate these emerging dynamics, ensuring that artificial intelligence acts as a cognitive amplifier rather than a replacement for human-centered communicative interaction.

items.title: Algorithmic Management, Employee Voice, and Procedural Justice: A Governance Framework for Accountable AI-Assisted Organizations
items.abstract: Algorithmic systems increasingly allocate tasks, rank performance, flag anomalies, and recommend decisions that affect employment conditions. This critical integrative review examines how algorithmic management may reshape employee voice and perceptions of procedural justice in AI-assisted organizations. It distinguishes automated recommendations from fully automated decisions, information disclosure from effective contestability, and worker participation from symbolic consultation. Established research on algorithmic control, organizational justice, algorithmic transparency, and human-AI decision structures provides the conceptual basis. The article develops an accountability chain linking data provenance, decision rights, reviewability, employee explanation, correction pathways, and evaluation of organizational outcomes. It argues that the mere presence of a human reviewer does not demonstrate meaningful oversight; review authority, adequate information, and the ability to change an outcome are separate requirements. Potential benefits of automation include consistency and early detection of harmful errors, while risks include opaque sanctions, strategic data manipulation, and the displacement of responsibility. No primary interviews, experimental observations, or quantitative effect estimates are reported. The proposed empirical agenda combines process tracing, employee surveys, decision-log audits, scenario-based experiments, and organizational comparisons. The framework can be supported only if its specified safeguards improve measurable fairness, accuracy, employee trust, and organizational performance beyond existing governance practices. algorithmic management; employee voice; procedural justice; AI governance; human oversight; organizational accountability

items.title: AN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE INTEGRATED PEDAGOGICAL PERSPECTIVE OF SECONDARY SCHOOL TEACHERS: A PHENOMENOLOGICAL STUDY
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is making a swift impact on the processes of teaching and learning by influencing lesson development, student assessment methods, and teachers’ perceptions of their profession. However, existing literature primarily focuses on the technical aspects of AI technologies rather than examining how secondary school teachers actually use these technologies when preparing lessons. The purpose of this study is to explore the experiences of secondary school teachers in using AI technologies in their teaching practices. Purposive sampling will be employed to select 15–20 teachers working with students in Grades 9–12 who have been using AI technologies for at least one semester. Data will be collected through semi-structured interviews and analyzed using content analysis. The findings are expected to provide a detailed understanding of teachers’ perceptions of AI integration into their professional practices, its influence on teaching and learning processes, the challenges and benefits they encounter, and the extent to which the use of AI tools shapes their professional identities.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) AND CHANGE MANAGEMENT IMPLEMENTATION IN THE NIGERIAN OIL AND GAS BUSINESS ENVIRONMENT
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) and change management implementation in the Nigerian oil and gas business environment. Focusing on three dimensions of AI (predictive analytics, robotic process automation, and AI-enhanced decision support systems), the study investigates how these technologies influence the effectiveness of change management initiatives within the Nigerian upstrea petroleum sector. Anchored in the Technology Acceptance Model (Davis, 1989) and the Dynamic Capabilities Theory (Teece et al., 1997), the research adopts a cross-sectional survey design, drawing data from 98 valid respondents comprising managerial and technical employees across 15 oil and gas firms in Rivers State, Nigeria. Using Pearson Product-Moment Correlation Coefficient (PPMC) and Multiple Regression Analysis, findings reveal strong, positive, and statistically significant relationships between all three AI dimensions and change management implementation. AI-enhanced decision support systems and predictive analytics emerged as the strongest predictors of change management outcomes. The regression model accounts for 64.3% of the variance in change management implementation, underscoring the substantial explanatory power of AI technologies in organizational transformation. The study recommends that Nigerian oil and gas firms strategically invest in AI infrastructure, build AI-competent workforces, and align AI deployment with their change management frameworks to enhance transition effectiveness and sustain competitive advantage in a rapidly evolving industry. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Change Management Implementation, Decision Support Systems, Nigerian Oil and Gas, Predictive Analytics, Robotic Process Automation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Social Inequality: A Review of Algorithmic Bias, Digital Exclusion, and Governance Responses
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into employment, education, healthcare, financial services, public administration, and social welfare systems, creating opportunities to improve efficiency, accessibility, and decision-making. However, the growing reliance on AI also raises concerns about social inequality, particularly when algorithmic systems reproduce existing patterns of discrimination, exclude marginalized populations, or concentrate technological benefits among already advantaged groups. This review examines the relationship between AI and social inequality, focusing on algorithmic bias, digital exclusion, and emerging governance responses. It synthesizes conceptual and empirical literature on discriminatory data practices, unequal access to digital infrastructure, disparities in AI literacy, and the socioeconomic consequences of automated decision-making. The review also examines how inequalities associated with gender, race, socioeconomic status, disability, geography, and language can influence the design, deployment, and outcomes of AI systems. The literature indicates that algorithmic discrimination may arise from unrepresentative datasets, historical inequalities embedded in training data, inappropriate performance measures, and insufficient institutional accountability. Digital exclusion further limits the capacity of disadvantaged populations to benefit from AI-enabled services, particularly in contexts characterized by inadequate connectivity, limited digital skills, affordability constraints, and linguistic barriers. Although regulatory frameworks, algorithmic audits, inclusive design, and human oversight offer important safeguards, their effectiveness depends on implementation, transparency, and meaningful participation by affected communities. The review argues that addressing AI-related social inequality requires an integrated approach combining technical fairness, digital inclusion, institutional accountability, and rights-based governance. It concludes that AI should be evaluated not only in terms of technological performance but also according to its contribution to social justice, equitable access, and inclusive development.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Anesthesiology: A Comprehensive Narrative Review
items.abstract: Background: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies in anesthesiology has emerged as a transformative force in perioperative medicine. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence on AI applications across the perioperative continuum. The objective is to provide a comprehensive overview of AI applications in anesthesiology, examining current implementations, clinical outcomes, and future directions across preoperative assessment, intraoperative monitoring, drug delivery, postoperative care, and clinical documentation. Methods: A systematic literature search was performed across several databases for peer-reviewed publications on AI applications in anesthesiology from 2015 to June, 2025. If the papers were peer reviewed and come from quality journals. Sixty-six papers from reputable peer-reviewed medical journals of high quality were selected for analysis. Results: The use of AI-based applications for anesthesiology can be summarized into 5 specific domains: predictive modeling to predict surgical risk assessment, real-time monitoring systems that measure anesthesia depth, automated drug delivery systems (and devices), postoperative complication prediction after surgery, and natural language processing (NLP) to assess clinical documentation. Recent advances show better patient outcomes, clinical decision-making and operational efficiency. Conclusion: AI technology holds substantial potential to enhance anesthesiology practice along the entire perioperative continuum. Although some challenges need to be addressed in respect of clinical integration and validation, we believe that there is sufficient evidence to justify undertaking further development work with a view towards implementation of AI-assisted anesthesia care.

items.title: Artificial intelligence applications in long-term care facilities: a scoping review across planning, design, operation, and assessment
items.abstract: Introduction Improving the quality of long-term care facilities (LTCFs) is critical to safeguarding the health, safety, dignity, and quality of life of older adults amid global population aging. However, traditional design methods for LTCFs rely heavily on static codes and empirical judgment, limiting their ability to respond to dynamic care needs and balance multiple objectives across lifecycle stages. To address these limitations, artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising solution through dynamic optimization and intelligent decision-making. Methods A scoping review was conducted to systematically map the applications of AI in LTCFs across four lifecycle stages: planning and site selection, architectural design, operation and management, and assessment and retrofit. Searches were performed in Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, SAGE Journals, and CNKI for literature published between January 2010 and December 2025, resulting in the inclusion of 38 eligible publications. The review was guided by the methodological framework proposed by Arksey and O’Malley and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Results Four main application pathways were identified, including prediction and evaluation, generation and evolution, sensing and recognition, and simulation and modeling. Specifically, AI was applied to site-selection evaluation and demand forecasting during planning; spatial layout generation and intelligent equipment integration during design; safety monitoring, behavior recognition, and environmental control during operation; and comfort and safety assessment and retrofit optimization during assessment. Research was concentrated in operation and management, whereas evidence on assessment and retrofit remained limited. Discussion Overall, AI shows potential to shift LTCFs from static, fragmented, and experience-based practices toward more data-informed, adaptive, and person-centered care environments. However, implementation remains constrained by data quality and standardization, facility heterogeneity, system integration, equitable access, privacy, and ethical concerns. This review provides planners, architects, engineers, care providers, facility managers, and public health decision-makers with a technology roadmap and identifies priorities for using AI-enabled built environments to support high-quality older adult care and sustainable long-term care systems.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence As A Learning Partner: Rethinking The Roles Of Teachers, Learners, And Knowledge Construction In Contemporary Education
items.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has transformed how teachers and students access, process, and construct knowledge in contemporary education. The increasing capacity of AI systems to provide information, generate ideas, support dialogue, and offer feedback raises fundamental questions about the changing roles of teachers and students and the position of AI within the learning process. This study aims to analyze the conceptualization of AI as a learning partner and examine its implications for teacher roles, student agency, and knowledge construction. This qualitative study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) with thematic-conceptual synthesis. Relevant literature was identified through Google Scholar, supported by Consensus as a supplementary literature discovery and verification tool. The reviewed literature was analyzed through thematic coding, categorization, comparison, and conceptual synthesis. The findings indicate two major patterns. First, the involvement of AI shifts the role of teachers from primary transmitters of information toward pedagogical guides, knowledge curators, dialogue facilitators, and validators of information and educational values, while students are increasingly positioned as active agents who question, evaluate, interpret, and reflect on AI-generated information. Second, knowledge construction becomes more relational, involving the interaction of teachers, students, and AI through processes of generation, verification, interpretation, negotiation, and reflection. AI therefore functions as a cognitive learning partner rather than a final epistemic authority. The study contributes a conceptual framework that integrates the teacher as a pedagogical agent, the student as an epistemic agent, and AI as a cognitive partner while maintaining human agency at the center of education.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE AS A TOOL FOR PERSONALIZED ENGLISH LANGUAGE LEARNING
items.abstract: Traditional language education classrooms often struggle to accommodate the diverse learning paces, styles, and proficiency levels of individual students. This research paper explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a transformative mechanism for personalized English language learning in higher education. By analyzing various AI-driven educational applications, intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), and adaptive learning platforms, this study examines how technology customizes linguistic input, provides real-time corrective feedback, and establishes individualized learning pathways. Utilizing a mixed-methods approach, the study surveys 120 undergraduate students to measure their engagement and perceived language acquisition progress when utilizing AI tools. The findings demonstrate that AI significantly enhances learner autonomy and vocabulary retention by adapting to the student's unique Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD). However, the paper also addresses critical limitations, including the lack of socio-cultural nuance in AI communication and the risk of reduced authentic interpersonal interaction. The study concludes with practical recommendations for integrating adaptive AI platforms into university EFL curricula to foster an optimized, student-centered learning environment.

items.title: Artificial intelligence at work: a socio-psychological model of employee adoption and innovation
items.abstract: Purpose This research aims to identify the key organisational, cognitive, and psychological predictors of perceived usefulness of artificial intelligence (AI) and to evaluate their influence on the AI adoption intention and innovative behavior of employees in the Jordanian setting. Design/methodology/approach A strict quantitative research design was adopted in the current study in which a structured online questionnaire was conducted among employees working in various industries in Jordan, mainly IT, retail, and banking. Quantitative data comprising 388 valid responses were then analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling to assess both the direct effects as well as moderating relationships between the constructs of interest. Findings The results show that organizational culture (β = 0.216), technology usage habits (β = 0.278), and AI self-image (β = 0.195) positively influence AI perceived usefulness, while AI literacy significantly reduces AI anxiety (β = −0.482). AI perceived usefulness strongly predicts employee innovative behavior (β = 0.608) and AI adoption intention (β = 0.657). Job insecurity weakens the relationship between perceived usefulness and adoption intention (β = −0.234), but its moderating effect on innovative behavior is insignificant. AI anxiety also weakens the effects of perceived usefulness on adoption intention (β = −0.208) and innovative behavior (β = −0.180). Originality/value A socio-psychological approach is used in this investigation, highlighting the significance of identity congruence and the importance of affective processes in the adoption of AI. It anticipates psychological and emotional engagement of employees in AI, breaking the false belief that acceptance is dictated by technical or rational factors only.
